replacement: 1. I will now close my eyes, stop my ears and turn my senses away from their objects. I will even wipe from my consciousness all the images of corporeal things; or, since that can hardly be done, I will at least regard them as empty and false. Holding conversation only with myself and examining my nature closely, I will try to gain, step by step, a more intimate and familiar knowledge of myself. I am a thinking (conscious) thing, that is, a being who doubts, affirms, denies, knows a few things and is ignorant of many — [who loves, hates], wills, refuses, and who also imagines and perceives. For, as I remarked before, the things I perceive or imagine are perhaps nothing at all apart from me [and in themselves]; yet I am assured that those modes of consciousness I call perceptions and imaginations exist in me, but only insofar as they are modes of consciousness.

replacement: 11. And finally, even if I granted that they proceeded from those objects, it does not necessarily follow that they must be like them. On the contrary, I have observed in many cases a great difference between the object and its idea. For example, I find in my mind two wholly different ideas of the sun. One, by which it appears extremely small, derives from the senses and should be placed among adventitious ideas. The other, by which it seems many times larger than the whole earth, is adopted on astronomical grounds, that is, drawn out of certain notions born with me, or else framed by myself in some other way. These two ideas certainly cannot both resemble the same sun; and reason teaches me that the one which seems to have come most directly from it is the most unlike.

replacement: 21. Among the clear and distinct ideas of corporeal things, there are some which, as it appears to me, might have been taken from the idea I have of myself: those of substance, duration, number and the like. When I think that a stone is a substance, or a thing capable of existing of itself, and that I am also a substance, I conceive that I am a thinking and non-extended thing and that the stone, on the contrary, is extended and unconscious, so that there is the greatest diversity between the two concepts; yet these two ideas seem to have this in common, that they both represent substances. In the same way, when I think of myself as existing now, recall that I existed some time ago, and am conscious of various thoughts whose number I know, I acquire the ideas of duration and number, which I can afterward transfer to as many objects as I please. As for the other qualities that make up the ideas of corporeal objects, namely extension, figure, situation and motion, it is true that they are not in me formally, since I am merely a thinking being. But because they are only certain modes of substance, and I myself am a substance, it seems possible that they may be contained in me eminently.
